newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Clinton dedicates Marshall monument, thousands cheer.
newsitem.headline: Clinton dedicates Marshall monument, thousands cheer.

text.p: As U.S. and Dutch flags fluttered in the setting sun, several thousand people flocked to a dockside plaza in this bustling seaport on Wednesday night to say thank you for the U.S. Marshall Plan that helped rebuild their city, and much of Western Europe, after World War Two.

Many more stood on a soaring steel bridge overlooking the harbour to watch as President Bill Clinton dedicated a monument to George C. Marshall, the U.S. military leader and diplomat who proposed the post-war reconstruction plan 50 years ago.

Over the next five years, $13 billion in U.S. aid -- an estimated $88 billion in today's money -- flowed to Europe, much of it via Rotterdam's port, in what British Prime Minister Winston Churchill called "the most unsordid act in history."

After meeting European leaders in The Hague and making a formal speech to mark the occasion, Clinton slipped away to Rotterdam for a campaign rally-style celebration, and to the pottery town of Delft for some sightseeing and pancakes.
In Rotterdam, Mayor Bram Peper said that in 1947 his city lay in ruins and offered Clinton his thanks for its massive reconstruction.

"Today the port of Rotterdam is the largest in the world," he said, with a sweeping gesture at the harbour bordered by towering modern buildings of glass and steel. "We couldn't have done it without the help of the American people."

Clinton, who was less than a year old when the Marshall Plan was launched, clearly relished what for him was one of the brightest moments of a three-nation European trip clouded by a Supreme Court ruling that an embarrassing sexual harassment lawsuit against him can go forward while he is still in office.
In Rotterdam, he urged the crowd to honour the Marshall Plan by helping the new democracies in Central and Eastern Europe become part of a continent that is united and free.
"Our purpose must be to summon the spirit of the Marshall generation to create a structure of opportunity and freedom and security for the next 50 years and beyond," he said.
"To give the young people here in this crowd tonight, throughout Europe, and in the rest of the world ... the chance to grow up and live out their dreams," he added.

The celebration had the air of a U.S. political rally, with a youth choir singing the signature song from Clinton's 1992 run for the presidency -- Fleetwood Mac's "Don't Stop Thinking About Tomorrow" -- and the release of hundreds of red, white and blue balloons in to the sky.
Clinton and his wife Hillary, who wore a matching pink suit and cloak, swayed in time with the music and then shook hands enthusiastically with the crowd.
After the celebration, Clinton stopped his motorcade in Delft, where he took a stroll, gazed at some of the city's famous china through a shop window, and then stopped in a restaurant.
Alain Soltany, the waiter who served the Clintons at "The Shield of Delft," said the president ate a traditional Dutch pancake with strawberries, and his wife one with cherries.
A large crowd gathered on Delft's main square to watch the president, who waved to them through the lead glass windows by his table on the restaurant's upper level.

Although the crowds were clearly delighted to catch a glimpse of the president, not everyone was impressed by his choice of restaurant. "It's only for tourists. I wouldn't eat here," said Willem Van den Bosch, a 49-year old antique dealer.
Afterwards, the Clintons walked across the square as Secret Service agents and Dutch police struggled to keep the crowds away, and took a tour of the Delft cathedral.
On Thursday, Clinton is scheduled to fly to London to meet British Prime Minister Tony Blair. He returns to Washington early on Friday morning.
